metadata.title: FermatMind IQ Test Guide: 30 Questions and Results
metadata.description: How to use FermatMind's original 30-question visual reasoning practice, read accuracy, distinguish simulated Beta from population scores, and understand limits.

faq_items.question: How many questions are in the FermatMind IQ test, and how long does it take?
faq_items.answer: The current public entry uses an original 30-question visual reasoning practice form. Allow about 20 minutes; this is an estimate, not a countdown limit confirmed by this guide. Actual time varies with pace and device. The current interface requires a selected option before continuing to the next question. Select an answer for all 30 questions, then submit through the interface and view the result.

faq_items.question: Is the result a formal IQ score?
faq_items.answer: No. It is not a formal clinical, educational, or credentialing result, an official Raven assessment, or evidence of Mensa eligibility. 18/30 = 60% is accuracy on this attempt. The simulated Beta cannot replace population IQ or a percentile, and this guide does not promise a displayed Beta. Do not invent a standard score or rank when an eligible population reference is unavailable.

faq_items.question: Can you include results in your resume or application materials?
faq_items.answer: Do not present the result as a qualification in a resume or application. It is not an accredited credential recognized by the target organization and cannot replace formal evidence of capability.

faq_items.question: Will doing it a few more times be more accurate?
faq_items.answer: Short-term repetition may lead to familiarity and practice effects. When retesting, record intervals, environments, and test item familiarity; do not interpret changes in scores directly as changes in intelligence.

faq_items.question: Does a low score mean you're not intelligent?
faq_items.answer: No. A low score on one online practice set does not establish low intelligence; the result is affected by question type, timing, current state, device, and prior experience, and it does not comprehensively assess cognitive ability.
